Write a cold outreach email from me to [prospect name/title] at [company name].
I run [your business — one sentence description]. I want to offer them [your service/product]. The email should be under 120 words, open with something specific about their company (use this detail: [something you noticed about them — a recent launch, blog post, hiring page, etc.]), clearly state what I do and why it matters to them, and end with a low-friction CTA like booking a 15-minute call. Tone: confident but not salesy. No fluff, no "I hope this email finds you well."
column3: 1. Cold Outreach Email That Actually Gets Replies

column2:
Write a 3-email follow-up sequence for a prospect who hasn't responded to my initial outreach. 
Context: I originally pitched them on [what you pitched]. Space the emails 3 days, 5 days, and 10 days apart. Email 1 should be a short nudge with a new angle or added value. Email 2 should share a quick case study or result: [paste a result or testimonial you've gotten]. Email 3 should be a polite breakup email that leaves the door open. Keep each under 80 words. Subject lines included.

I sell [your product/service] at [price point/range]. My ideal client is [describe — industry, size, problem, budget]. Create a set of 10 qualifying questions I can ask on a discovery call to determine if someone is a good fit. For each question, include: the question itself, what I'm really trying to learn (the hidden intent), and red flags vs. green flags in their answer. Order them from rapport-building to deal-qualifying. The conversation should feel natural, not like an interrogation.

Create a pricing proposal template I can reuse for my [service type] business. I typically offer: [describe your service tiers or packages — e.g., "a basic, standard, and premium package"]. For each tier, I need placeholders for: tier name, what's included, what's not included, timeline, price, and payment terms. Also include: (1) A "Why these prices?" section that frames the investment around ROI not cost, (2) An "investment comparison" that shows what this would cost if they hired in-house or used a more expensive agency, (3) Optional add-ons section with individual pricing, (4) Terms & next steps. Make the premium tier look like the obvious best value.

Write an email to [client name] asking for referrals after a successful project. We just finished [describe the project and result]. I'm looking for more clients like them — specifically [describe ideal referral: industry, size, problem]. Make the ask specific: "Do you know anyone who [specific situation]?" Offer something in return if applicable: [referral bonus, free month, gift, or just genuine gratitude]. Include a forwardable blurb they can send to their contact. Under 120 words.

Write a professional but firm email response to a client who just asked me to do [describe the extra work they requested] which is outside our original agreement of [describe original scope]. I want to maintain the relationship but set a clear boundary. Offer two options: (1) we add it to scope at an additional cost of [your price], or (2) we table it for a Phase 2. Tone: warm, professional, zero pushover energy.
column3: 3. Client Response to a Scope Creep Request

column2:
Write a weekly status update email to [client name] for the [project name] project. Here's what happened this week:
[Paste your raw notes — tasks completed, blockers, metrics, etc.]
Structure it as: (1) Summary (2-3 sentences of the big picture), (2) Completed This Week (bullet points), (3) In Progress (bullet points with expected completion), (4) Blockers or Needs from Client (if any), (5) Plan for Next Week. Tone: professional, concise, shows I'm on top of things.
